questions.q: Write the chemical formula of bleaching powder and state the two raw materials used in its industrial preparation.
questions.a: Correct answer: Bleaching powder is CaOCl₂ (calcium oxychloride). It is prepared by passing chlorine gas over dry slaked lime [Ca(OH)₂]. A wrong answer like "CaCl₂" or "Ca(OCl)₂" reveals confusion between bleaching powder and calcium chloride/calcium hypochlorite. Writing "wet slaked lime" instead of "dry slaked lime" shows ignorance of the critical condition that moisture hydrolyses the product.

questions.q: Why does baking soda (NaHCO₃) release CO₂ when heated, while washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) does not? Explain using the concept of thermal decomposition.
questions.a: Correct answer: Baking soda is a hydrogen carbonate (HCO₃⁻) which decomposes on heating to give carbonate (CO₃²⁻), water, and CO₂: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂↑. Washing soda is already a carbonate (CO₃²⁻) and only loses water of crystallisation on heating, not CO₂. A student who says "both give CO₂" or "washing soda gives CO₂ because it has carbonate" confuses the thermal stability of carbonate vs hydrogen carbonate ions.

questions.q: A student heats 16.8 g of baking soda (NaHCO₃) strongly until constant mass. Calculate the mass of solid residue left and the volume of CO₂ gas evolved at STP. (Molar masses: NaHCO₃ = 84 g/mol, Na₂CO₃ = 106 g/mol, CO₂ = 44 g/mol; molar volume at STP = 22.4 L/mol)
questions.a:
Step 1: Write balanced equation: 2NaHCO₃(s) → Na₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(g) + CO₂(g).
Step 2: Moles of NaHCO₃ = 16.8 g / 84 g/mol = 0.2 mol.
Step 3: From stoichiometry, 2 mol NaHCO₃ give 1 mol Na₂CO₃ and 1 mol CO₂. So 0.2 mol NaHCO₃ gives 0.1 mol Na₂CO₃ and 0.1 mol CO₂.
Step 4: Mass of Na₂CO₃ residue = 0.1 mol × 106 g/mol = 10.6 g.
Step 5: Volume of CO₂ at STP = 0.1 mol × 22.4 L/mol = 2.24 L.
Answer: Residue = 10.6 g; CO₂ volume = 2.24 L.
A wrong mass (e.g., 16.8 g or 5.3 g) reveals inability to use stoichiometric coefficients; wrong volume (e.g., 4.48 L) shows forgetting the 2:1 mole ratio.

questions.q: Compare the chemical changes when plaster of Paris is mixed with water versus when washing soda is dissolved in water. Identify the type of change (chemical/physical) in each case and justify.
questions.a: Correct answer: Plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O) + water → Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) — a **chemical change** (exothermic, new substance with different crystal structure and hydration state). Washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) dissolving in water → aqueous Na₂CO₃ + water — a **physical change** (no new substance, only dissociation into ions, reversible by evaporation). A student calling both "physical" misses the irreversible setting reaction of plaster; calling both "chemical" fails to recognise that hydration of ions is physical.

questions.q: A label on a bottle reads "Bleaching Powder — 35% available chlorine". A student claims this means the sample contains 35% Cl₂ gas by mass. Evaluate this claim and explain what "available chlorine" actually means.
questions.a: The claim is **incorrect**. "Available chlorine" refers to the chlorine liberated as Cl₂ gas when bleaching powder is treated with excess acid (e.g., dilute H₂SO₄), measured as a percentage by mass. It does not mean free Cl₂ gas is present in the solid. The reaction: CaOCl₂ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + Cl₂↑. A 35% label means 100 g sample releases 35 g Cl₂ gas on acidification. A student who agrees with the claim confuses "available chlorine" (a measure of oxidising power) with actual Cl₂ content.

questions.q: Design a simple laboratory experiment to distinguish between samples of baking soda and washing soda using only dilute hydrochloric acid and lime water (calcium hydroxide solution). Write the observations and chemical equations.
questions.a:
Procedure: Take two test tubes, add a spatula of each powder, add dilute HCl, and pass the gas evolved through lime water.
Observation for baking soda: Brisk effervescence, gas turns lime water milky (CO₂).
Observation for washing soda: Effervescence, gas turns lime water milky (CO₂) — **but slower because washing soda is a stronger base and reacts less vigorously? Actually both give CO₂ with acid. Wait, washing soda (Na₂CO₃) + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Baking soda: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Both give CO₂. So this test does NOT distinguish them.**
Better test: Heat a small amount of each in a dry test tube. Baking soda decomposes giving CO₂ (turns lime water milky) and leaves Na₂CO₃ residue. Washing soda only loses water of crystallisation (condensation on cooler part of tube), no CO₂.
A good answer uses thermal decomposition, not acid test. A poor answer uses acid test and claims difference in rate, showing lack of understanding that both carbonates/hydrogen carbonates give CO₂ with acid.
